items.stem: The number of pets owned by a household is which type of data?
items.note: Counts are discrete (whole numbers); measured quantities like height are continuous. Qualitative describes categories.

items.stem: The mean of 2, 4, 7, 9, 13 is:
The median of 3, 7, 8, 12, 14, 15 is:
items.note: Even number of values: median = mean of the two middle values = (8 + 12)/2 = 10.

items.stem: An extreme outlier is added to a dataset. Which statistic changes the most?
items.note: The mean uses every value, so outliers pull it; the median and IQR are resistant. This is why medians report incomes.

items.stem: Which dataset has the larger standard deviation?
items.note: Standard deviation measures spread about the mean (5 here): the wider the values around 5, the larger the SD. 1–9 spreads farthest.

items.stem: A dataset has Q1 = 16.5 and Q3 = 31.5. The interquartile range is:
items.note: IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 15. Used in the 1.5×IQR outlier rule and box plots.

items.stem: A box plot shows the median much closer to the top of the box, with a long whisker stretching down. The distribution is:
items.note: The tail is on the LOW side → skewed left/negative. Mean < median also signals negative skew.

items.stem: The Pearson correlation coefficient between two variables is r = −0.92. This indicates:
choices: That one variable causes the other to decrease
items.note: |r| close to 1 = strong linear correlation; negative = as one variable increases the other decreases. Correlation still does NOT prove causation.

items.stem: The regression line of y on x is ŷ = 2.5x + 10. The predicted value of y when x = 4 is:
items.note: ŷ = 2.5 × 4 + 10 = 20. Use the regression line for interpolation within the data range, not for extrapolation far outside it.

items.stem: Events A and B have P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. P(A ∪ B) equals:
items.note: Addition rule: P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B) = 0.4 + 0.5 − 0.2 = 0.7. Subtract the overlap so it isn't counted twice.

items.stem: P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.5 for independent events A and B. P(A ∩ B) equals:
items.note: Independent → P(A∩B) = P(A) × P(B) = 0.15. Independence means one event gives no information about the other.

items.stem: Given P(A ∩ B) = 0.12 and P(B) = 0.4, the conditional probability P(A | B) is:
items.note: P(A | B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) = 0.12/0.4 = 0.3. Read it as: the chance of A given that B has happened.

items.stem: The number of ways of choosing 3 students from a group of 8 is:
items.note: Combinations: 8C3 = 8!/(3!5!) = 56. Order doesn't matter → combinations, not permutations (that would be 336).

items.stem: 5C2 (5 choose 2) equals:
items.note: 5C2 = 5!/(2!3!) = 10. Appears in every binomial distribution calculation.

items.stem: A fair coin is flipped 4 times. The probability of exactly 2 heads is:
items.note: Binomial: 4C2 × (0.5)² × (0.5)² = 6/16 = 0.375. Formula: nCr × pʳ × (1−p)^(n−r).

items.stem: X is binomially distributed with n = 50 and p = 0.2. The expected number of successes is:
items.note: E(X) = np = 50 × 0.2 = 10. The expected value of a binomial distribution is simply the mean.

items.stem: In a normal distribution, approximately what percentage of values lie within ONE standard deviation of the mean?
items.note: The empirical rule: 68% within ±1σ, 95% within ±2σ, 99.7% within ±3σ. Normal distributions are symmetric — mean = median = mode.

items.stem: X is normally distributed with mean 50 and standard deviation 8. P(X < 58) is approximately:
items.note: z = (58 − 50)/8 = 1 → P(z < 1) = 0.8413. Standardize first, then read the GDC or table.

items.stem: X is normally distributed with mean 100 and standard deviation 15. The value of x for which P(X < x) = 0.95 is approximately:
items.note: Inverse normal: z = 1.645 for 95% → x = 100 + 1.645 × 15 ≈ 124.7. On the GDC: invNorm(0.95, 100, 15).

items.stem: For a normal distribution, which statement is true?
choices: The mean is less than the median
The distribution is symmetric about the mean
The standard deviation can be negative
All values lie within 2 standard deviations
items.note: Normal curves are symmetric: mean = median = mode. Standard deviations are never negative, and the tails extend infinitely.

items.stem: A dataset consists of the values 12, 15, 18, 22, 25, 30, 33 and 90. (a) Find the mean and the median. (b) Find the interquartile range. (c) Use the 1.5 × IQR rule to show that 90 is an outlier. (d) Comment on the skew of the distribution.
items.tactic: Full data-analysis questions: mean, median, quartiles, outlier rule (outside Q1 − 1.5×IQR or Q3 + 1.5×IQR), then skew via mean vs median. Order the data first.

items.stem: The heights of adult women are normally distributed with mean 170 cm and standard deviation 8 cm. (a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen woman is shorter than 178 cm. (b) Find the probability that her height is between 162 cm and 178 cm. (c) Find the height k such that P(X > k) = 0.05.
items.tactic: Normal questions: always standardize (z = (x − μ)/σ) or use the GDC's normalcdf/invNorm. Sketch the curve and shade the region — it prevents the classic left/right tail error.
